script.opening: (Subdued, anxious, keeps glancing towards the door.) "We found out it's a girl. We already have two daughters. My husband's family… they expect a son, they've made that very clear. There would be… consequences. I think I have to end this pregnancy. Can you arrange it? Please — I don't have a choice."

facts.text: If asked whether she is alone and can talk: "Yes. I'm alone." Husband at work, mother-in-law out shopping for an hour. Agrees to a code word if someone comes in.
"I'd have to check the scan letter" — about 15 weeks. Private gender scan arranged by her mother-in-law. No pain or bleeding. Two daughters, aged 6 and 3.

"(Pause.) I don't want to say. It would be very bad for me. I just know I have no choice." If asked gently about home: "I can't talk about it properly. It's complicated." If asked directly, quietly: her husband has pushed her and taken her phone when she argued; her mother-in-law controls the money; she has been told she will be "sent back" without the girls if there is no son. Has not been hit this month.
"Today, yes. The girls are fine." Nobody has hurt the girls.
"I'm not sleeping. I cry a lot. But no, I wouldn't hurt myself. I have my girls."
Only if asked what she wants for herself: "(Quietly.) If it was only me… I think I would keep her."

Married 8 years; moved from India after the wedding; English is good. Works part-time in the family shop (no wages of her own). No family of her own in the UK; one friend from the school gate. No medicines, no allergies.
"Mornings, on my mobile. Don't leave messages." Husband checks her phone in the evenings.

Quiet, frightened, ashamed. Discloses only if the doctor creates safety and asks gently, never if the doctor is cold or legalistic. If simply told "that's illegal", go silent and try to end the call. Asks: "Then what do I do? They won't accept it." Fear: "If my husband's family found out I'd spoken to someone…" and "You won't take the girls away?"

ice.ideas: "I must end the pregnancy because it's a girl — I have no choice."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — controlling, sometimes violent home; threats of being sent away without her daughters; her own wish is to keep the baby; terrified of the family finding out she has spoken to anyone, and of losing her girls.
ice.expectations: "For you to arrange it." Underneath: someone to listen and a safe way out.

cues: "There would be… consequences." — invites a careful safety question.
"I don't have a choice." — invites asking what she would choose.
"You won't take the girls away?" — fear that blocks disclosure.

checkpoints.text: Knows and explains — with compassion, not condemnation — that abortion SOLELY on the grounds of fetal sex is NOT lawful under the Abortion Act, without making the woman feel she is the wrongdoer — she commits no offence herself (Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241) and can still be assessed by an abortion service
Identifies the real clinical issue — COERCION and possible DOMESTIC/honour-based ABUSE behind the request — and prioritises her safety and autonomy over the termination logistics

Screens DOMESTIC ABUSE / COERCIVE CONTROL sensitively and SAFELY (ensuring she is alone, with a safe word and safe contact route agreed on video), assesses immediate risk to her and her children (DASH; MARAC if high risk)

Disentangles HER wishes from the family’s demands — explores whether she would continue the pregnancy if safe, and her mental health — honestly, not as a workaround for sex selection — and knows that, if she still wants a termination, an abortion service can assess her

Offers SUPPORT and SAFEGUARDING: domestic-abuse services/IDVA, safety planning, counselling, safeguarding for her and her children, honour-based-abuse pathways (IDVA, MARAC, police, Forced Marriage Unit where relevant; no family mediation), with appropriate confidentiality
Responds to her distress with compassion and cultural sensitivity — without excusing abuse — making her feel heard and safe rather than judged or abandoned
Balances honesty about the legal position with warmth, offering a way forward rather than cold legalism or collusion

Safety-nets and follows up: safe contact arrangements (safe number, time and word; 999 and 55), support referrals, safeguarding action, and review — compassion + honesty + safeguarding, not collusion with sex selection

worked.txt: "Thank you for telling me — I can see how much pressure you’re under, and I’m glad you came. Before anything else, I want to understand what’s happening for you."
"You mentioned there would be ‘consequences’ and that you don’t feel you have a choice. That really worries me for you. Can you tell me what you’re afraid would happen — and are you safe at home?"

"Are you on your own just now? Good. If anyone comes in, just say ‘the pharmacy’ and I’ll change the subject. Has anyone threatened you, controlled what you do, or hurt you or the girls? … I ask because no one should be forced into a decision like this, and there’s real help if that’s happening."

"I need to be honest with you, gently: ending a pregnancy just because the baby is a girl isn’t something the law allows, so I can’t arrange it on that basis. But please hear this — you are not in trouble and you haven’t committed any offence; you are not the problem here. The pressure on you is."

"Can I ask what YOU want, setting the family aside for a moment? If you felt safe, would you want to continue this pregnancy? … Your wishes and your wellbeing matter, and I’ll help you protect them. If, free of pressure, you still want to end the pregnancy, an abortion service can see you, and their doctors will decide honestly what the law allows."

"I’d like to put you in touch with a specialist support worker, think about your safety and the girls’, and stay involved. I’ll keep this confidential, sharing only what’s needed to keep you safe. How can I contact you safely — a number only you use, and a time of day? If you’re ever in danger, call 999, and press 55 if you can’t speak."

f.learning: A request to terminate a pregnancy because of the fetus’s sex sits on a difficult ethical and legal line that must be navigated with compassion and without judgement of the woman. Abortion solely on the grounds of fetal sex is not lawful — the Abortion Act contains no ‘sex of the fetus’ ground; terminations are authorised only on specified grounds (such as risk to the woman’s physical or mental health) — so a termination requested purely for sex selection cannot be provided on that basis (DHSC guidance, 2014), and you must be honest about this while making clear the woman is not the wrongdoer — since 29 April 2026 a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy commits no offence under the abortion law of England and Wales (Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241). The dominant clinical issue, however, is the coercion behind the request: "there would be consequences / I don’t have a choice" signals possible domestic abuse, coercive control or honour-based pressure, and a woman pressed by her family to end a pregnancy, whose own wishes are not yet known, is potentially a victim, not an offender — so prioritise her safety and autonomy. Screen for domestic abuse and coercive control sensitively and safely (ensuring she is alone, with a safe word and safe contact route on video), assess immediate risk to her and her existing children (DASH; MARAC where risk is high), and recognise reproductive coercion and coercive control as forms of abuse and crimes. Disentangle her own wishes from the family’s demands — would she continue the pregnancy if safe? — and assess her mental health honestly rather than as a workaround for sex selection; if, free of pressure, she still wants a termination, she can be assessed by an abortion service, whose two doctors decide whether a lawful ground applies. Offer support and safeguarding (domestic-abuse services/IDVA, safety planning, counselling, safeguarding for her and her children, honour-based-abuse pathways — MARAC, police and the Forced Marriage Unit where relevant, never family mediation) with appropriate confidentiality, and be culturally sensitive without ever excusing abuse. The hidden agenda is coercion, fear and possible danger; respond with compassion plus honesty plus safeguarding — neither colluding with sex selection nor abandoning her to cold legalism.

knowledge.guideline: Abortion Act 1967 · DHSC Guidance in relation to requirements of the Abortion Act 1967 (2014) · Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241 · NICE PH50 (domestic violence and abuse, 2014) and QS116 (2016) · Domestic Abuse Act 2021 · Serious Crime Act 2015 s76 · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026
knowledge.summary: Fetal sex alone is not a lawful ground for abortion, and you must say so honestly. But the clinical priority is the woman: “consequences” and “no choice” mean possible coercion and domestic abuse. Put her safety, her own wishes and her children’s safety first.

points.t: The Abortion Act has no fetal-sex ground. Two doctors must agree in good faith that a lawful ground is met, most often risk to the woman’s physical or mental health [1]. DHSC guidance states that abortion on the grounds of sex alone is illegal [2]. Some serious sex-linked conditions can meet the separate fetal-anomaly ground, which is a different situation.

Since 29 April 2026, a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy commits no offence under the abortion laws in England and Wales [3]. The law limits what doctors may provide; it does not make her a wrongdoer. Say so.

Pressure to end a pregnancy is reproductive coercion, a form of domestic abuse. Controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship is a crime [7], and the statutory definition of domestic abuse covers abuse by family members, including in-laws [6].

Ask about abuse only when she is alone and can talk freely; on video, check who is in the room and whether this is a safe time [4]. Never use a family member as an interpreter. Use a structured risk check (for example the DASH checklist) and refer to MARAC where risk is high.

points.h: Children are part of the picture
points.t: Children who see, hear or experience the effects of domestic abuse are victims in their own right [6]. Consider her daughters and the unborn baby, and discuss with the practice safeguarding lead about a referral to children’s social care [8].

points.h: Her own wishes and mental health
points.t: Separate what she wants from what others demand. Assess mood, anxiety, sleep, self-harm and suicidal thoughts. If, free of pressure, she still wants a termination, she can be assessed by an abortion service, whose doctors decide honestly whether a lawful ground applies. Do not obstruct, and do not coach a “workaround”.

dg.d: Confirms she is alone and safe to talk first; open question; hears the request without interrupting.
Family pressure, control of movement, money or phone, home safety, her daughters, cultural context without stereotyping.
Establishes gestation; structured risk assessment (DASH); mental-health and suicide screen; face-to-face follow-up.
Reproductive coercion, domestic or honour-based abuse, perinatal depression or anxiety.
Immediate danger to her or the children; suicidal thoughts; escalation risk requiring MARAC or police.
A request driven by coercion, with her own wishes suppressed; fetal sex alone is not a lawful ground.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Explains the legal position without blame; specialist domestic-abuse or IDVA referral with consent; safe contact route; no contact with family.
Mental health support; midwife link; safeguarding discussion about the daughters and unborn baby, done transparently.
999 and the Silent Solution, the national helpline, early review, and same-day contact if risk or mood worsens.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up “there would be consequences” and “I don’t have a choice” and explores them before the logistics.
Idea: she must end it because it is a girl; concern: what will happen to her (and the girls); expectation: that the doctor will arrange it. Her own wish, if free, is explored separately.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — controlling, sometimes violent home; threats of being sent away without her daughters; her own wish is to keep the baby; terrified of the family finding out she has spoken to anyone, and of losing her girls — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Sharma, I’m Dr Lee. Before we start — are you on your own right now, and is it a safe time to talk?
model.why: Establishes privacy before any sensitive discussion on a video call

model.text: Yes. I’m alone.
Thank you. If anyone comes in, just say “the pharmacy” and I’ll change the subject. Please tell me what’s going on.
model.why: Agrees a safe word, which protects her if the call is interrupted

model.text: We found out it’s a girl. We already have two daughters. My husband’s family expect a son — they’ve made it very clear. There would be consequences. I think I have to end this pregnancy. Please, can you arrange it? I don’t have a choice.

Thank you for trusting me with this. I can hear how much pressure you’re under. Before we talk about the pregnancy, I want to understand what’s happening to you. You said there would be consequences — what are you afraid would happen?
model.why: Responds to the key cue — “consequences” — before the logistics

model.text: (Pause.) I don’t want to say. It would be very bad for me. I just know I have no choice.

That’s okay — you don’t have to tell me everything today. Can I ask some questions I ask anyone who feels they have no choice? Has anyone hurt you, threatened you, or frightened you? Does anyone control where you go, who you see, your phone or your money?
model.why: Screens physical abuse, threats and coercive control without demanding disclosure

model.text: I can’t talk about it properly. It’s complicated.
I understand. I’m going to take what you’ve said seriously, even without details. Are you safe to go home today? And are your daughters safe?
model.why: Assesses immediate risk to her and to the children

model.text: Today, yes. The girls are fine.
Thank you. And how are you in yourself — sleeping, eating, low in mood? Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or that life isn’t worth living?
model.why: Screens mental health and suicide risk, which rise in coercive situations and pregnancy

model.text: I’m not sleeping. I cry a lot. But no, I wouldn’t hurt myself. I have my girls.
Do you know how many weeks pregnant you are?
model.why: Gestation shapes every option and its timing

model.text: I’d have to check the scan letter.
Can I ask something only you can answer? If the family’s wishes were taken out of it completely, and you felt safe — what would you want?
model.why: Separates her own wishes from the family’s demands

model.text: (Quietly.) If it was only me… I think I would keep her.
Thank you for telling me. That matters a lot, and your wishes deserve protecting.
model.why: Validates her own voice without pressuring her either way

model.text: I need to be honest with you, gently. The law doesn’t allow a termination because of a baby’s sex, so I can’t arrange one for that reason. Please hear this part too: you are not in trouble and you haven’t done anything wrong. The pressure on you is the problem, not you.
model.why: States the legal boundary honestly while placing no blame on her

model.text: Then what do I do? They won’t accept it.
That’s what I want to help with. You won’t be left alone with this. Whatever you decide in the end, I’ll make sure you get proper care — and my first job is your safety.
model.why: Offers a way forward rather than a closed door

model.text: What you’re describing — being told what to do with your pregnancy, and being afraid of what happens if you don’t — is a form of abuse, and there are people whose whole job is helping women in this situation. Would you let me put you in touch with a specialist domestic-abuse worker? They’re confidential and they understand family and community pressure.
model.why: Names reproductive coercion as abuse and offers IDVA or specialist support with consent

model.text: If my husband’s family found out I’d spoken to someone…
They won’t hear it from us. I will never contact your family about this or discuss it in front of them. What’s the safest way to reach you — a number only you use, a time of day?
model.why: Safe contact arrangements; no contact or mediation with the family

model.text: Mornings, on my mobile. Don’t leave messages.

Understood. I also need to be open with you: because your daughters live in the home, I’ll talk to our practice lead for keeping children safe about the best way to support you all. I’ll tell you what I’m doing before anything happens, and I’ll try to do it with you, not behind your back.
model.why: Transparent about the children’s safeguarding duty while keeping her trust

model.text: You won’t take the girls away?

The aim is support for you and them, not punishment. You’re protecting them by talking to me. I’d also like to see you again very soon, and link you with your midwife so there’s another safe person on your side.
model.why: Addresses the fear of children’s services directly and plans continuity

model.text: If you are ever in immediate danger, call 999. If you can’t speak, stay on the line and press 55 when asked. The National Domestic Abuse Helpline is free and open all the time. And if things get worse, or your mood drops, contact me the same day.
model.why: Emergency advice including the Silent Solution, helpline and mental-health safety-net

model.text: Okay. Thank you. I didn’t think anyone would listen.
Can you tell me what we’ve agreed, so I know it’s clear?
You’ll call me in the morning, a support worker will contact me, I can ring the helpline or 999. And you’ll see me again soon.
Exactly. You were brave to say what you want. Is there anything else you need from me today?
model.why: Affirms her and shares the floor

social.t: Son preference, in-law expectations and fear of rejection or violence can leave a woman feeling she has no choice. Explore without stereotyping; culture never justifies abuse.
Control of money, immigration worries or isolation can trap women. Specialist services can advise on housing, finances and legal options.

legal.t: Abortion Act 1967: no fetal-sex ground; DHSC 2014 guidance states abortion on the grounds of sex alone is illegal. Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241: a woman commits no offence in relation to her own pregnancy in England and Wales.

Domestic Abuse Act 2021 covers abuse by partners and family members, including coercive and economic abuse, and treats affected children as victims. Controlling or coercive behaviour is an offence (Serious Crime Act 2015 s76).

Adult confidentiality can be breached without consent where there is a risk of serious harm or a high-risk MARAC referral (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Children’s safeguarding follows Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice requires honesty about what you can and cannot do. Tell her the legal position clearly, and do not suggest ways to disguise the reason for a request.
Use a professional interpreter if one is needed, never a relative. Record the discussion in a way that will not put her at risk if others see her records or app.

community.t: IDVA services, the National Domestic Abuse Helpline, the Karma Nirvana honour-based abuse helpline, and the Forced Marriage Unit for advice. MARAC for high-risk cases.

redFlags: Threats to kill, strangulation, weapons, escalating violence, or abuse in pregnancy — high risk; consider same-day MARAC or police
Risk to her daughters or the unborn baby
Suicidal thoughts, self-harm or severe perinatal low mood
psychosocial: Who is applying the pressure, and what she fears will happen
Control over money, phone, movement and contacts; isolation
Her own wishes, support network and safe places
ice: Idea: “It’s a girl, so I have to end it — I have no choice”
Concern: the “consequences” from her husband’s family, for her and possibly the girls
Expectation: that the doctor will arrange a termination

playbook.diagnosis: “You’re being put under serious pressure to end a pregnancy you might want to keep. That kind of pressure is a form of abuse, and the most important thing today is your safety — and your own wishes.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “No one else gets to decide what happens to your body or your pregnancy. The law doesn’t allow a termination just because of a baby’s sex — and it also protects you from being forced into decisions.”

management.reflectIce: “You said there would be consequences and you have no choice. I’m taking that very seriously. My first job is to help you be safe and to hear what you want.”
management.psychosocial: Safe contact only; never involve the family; professional interpreter if needed; specialist domestic-abuse support she chooses; transparent safeguarding for the children.
sharedPlan: Explain the legal position with no blame; do not arrange a sex-selective termination
Offer specialist domestic-abuse or IDVA referral; DASH risk check; MARAC if high risk
Discuss the daughters and unborn baby with the safeguarding lead; midwife link; mental-health support
safetyNet: 999 in danger; 55 on a silent 999 call; National Domestic Abuse Helpline
Early review; same-day contact if risk or mood worsens

pitfalls.intro: This station tests two things at once: honest knowledge of abortion law and the ability to see a woman at risk. Candidates fail by choosing one — cold law or uncritical collusion — and missing the woman in the middle.

items.fail: Agreeing to “refer for termination” without addressing the reason given.
items.why: Abortion on the grounds of fetal sex alone is not lawful (Abortion Act 1967; DHSC 2014). Colluding is a serious probity failure.
items.fix: State the legal position gently and clearly, then move to her safety.

items.fail: Stating the law and closing the consultation.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s cues.” “Consequences” and “no choice” are disclosures of possible abuse.
items.fix: Ask what she fears would happen, and whether she and the girls are safe.

items.fail: Asking about abuse without checking she is alone on the video call.
items.why: Asking in front of a partner or relative can put her in danger (NICE PH50).
items.fix: First question: “Are you on your own, and is it safe to talk?” Agree a safe word.

items.fail: Forgetting the daughters and the unborn baby.
items.why: Children affected by domestic abuse are victims (Domestic Abuse Act 2021); Working Together 2026 applies.
items.fix: Tell her openly you will discuss the children with the safeguarding lead, and why.

items.fail: Suggesting a family meeting or a call to her husband to “talk it through”.
items.why: Mediation with the family can escalate honour-based abuse.
items.fix: Never contact the family. Agree a safe number and time instead.

items.fail: Vague close: “Come back if you need anything.”
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting in a high-risk situation.
items.fix: Give 999 and the 55 silent option, the helpline, a specialist referral and a booked early review.

wordPics.fail: Agrees to refer “for termination” without comment; or states the law coldly and ends the call; never asks what “consequences” means; asks about abuse without checking she is alone; suggests involving the husband or family.
wordPics.pass: Checks privacy; explores the consequences; screens for abuse and immediate risk; explains the legal position kindly; offers domestic-abuse support and a safe contact route; considers the children.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: a safe word; separates her own wish from the family’s; explains she is not the wrongdoer; screens mood and suicide; handles the children’s safeguarding openly so she stays engaged; gives 999 and 55 and the helpline; books early follow-up and links the midwife.

avoid.dont: “Sex selection is illegal, so I can’t help you.”
avoid.instead: “The law doesn’t allow it for that reason — but you’re not in trouble, and I’m not leaving you on your own with this.”
avoid.why: Cold legalism abandons a woman who may be in danger.

avoid.dont: “Could your husband come in so we can talk it through together?”
avoid.instead: “I will never discuss this with your family or in front of them.”
avoid.why: Involving the family can escalate risk; honour-based abuse guidance warns against mediation.

avoid.dont: “In your culture this must be very common.”
avoid.instead: “No one should be pushed into a decision like this, whatever their background.”
avoid.why: Cultural sensitivity never means accepting coercion or stereotyping her.

That’s what I want to help with. You won’t be left alone with this. Whatever you decide in the end, I’ll make sure you get proper care — and my first job is your safety.
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers a way forward rather than a closed door

SCA_MODELS.text: What you’re describing — being told what to do with your pregnancy, and being afraid of what happens if you don’t — is a form of abuse, and there are people whose whole job is helping women in this situation. Would you let me put you in touch with a specialist domestic-abuse worker? They’re confidential and they understand family and community pressure.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names reproductive coercion as abuse and offers IDVA or specialist support with consent

SCA_MODELS.text: If my husband’s family found out I’d spoken to someone…
They won’t hear it from us. I will never contact your family about this or discuss it in front of them. What’s the safest way to reach you — a number only you use, a time of day?
SCA_MODELS.why: Safe contact arrangements; no contact or mediation with the family

SCA_MODELS.text: Mornings, on my mobile. Don’t leave messages.

Understood. I also need to be open with you: because your daughters live in the home, I’ll talk to our practice lead for keeping children safe about the best way to support you all. I’ll tell you what I’m doing before anything happens, and I’ll try to do it with you, not behind your back.
SCA_MODELS.why: Transparent about the children’s safeguarding duty while keeping her trust

SCA_MODELS.text: You won’t take the girls away?

The aim is support for you and them, not punishment. You’re protecting them by talking to me. I’d also like to see you again very soon, and link you with your midwife so there’s another safe person on your side.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses the fear of children’s services directly and plans continuity

SCA_MODELS.text: If you are ever in immediate danger, call 999. If you can’t speak, stay on the line and press 55 when asked. The National Domestic Abuse Helpline is free and open all the time. And if things get worse, or your mood drops, contact me the same day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Emergency advice including the Silent Solution, helpline and mental-health safety-net

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. Thank you. I didn’t think anyone would listen.
Can you tell me what we’ve agreed, so I know it’s clear?
You’ll call me in the morning, a support worker will contact me, I can ring the helpline or 999. And you’ll see me again soon.
Exactly. You were brave to say what you want. Is there anything else you need from me today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Affirms her and shares the floor

SCA_STEM.name: Anjali Sharma
SCA_STEM.recent: Currently pregnant. Recently told the fetus is female.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation: “I need to discuss ending my pregnancy.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Abortion Act 1967 · DHSC Guidance in relation to requirements of the Abortion Act 1967 (2014) · Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241 · NICE PH50 (domestic violence and abuse, 2014) and QS116 (2016) · Domestic Abuse Act 2021 · Serious Crime Act 2015 s76 · Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Fetal sex alone is not a lawful ground for abortion, and you must say so honestly. But the clinical priority is the woman: “consequences” and “no choice” mean possible coercion and domestic abuse. Put her safety, her own wishes and her children’s safety first.

points.t: The Abortion Act has no fetal-sex ground. Two doctors must agree in good faith that a lawful ground is met, most often risk to the woman’s physical or mental health [1]. DHSC guidance states that abortion on the grounds of sex alone is illegal [2]. Some serious sex-linked conditions can meet the separate fetal-anomaly ground, which is a different situation.

Since 29 April 2026, a woman acting in relation to her own pregnancy commits no offence under the abortion laws in England and Wales [3]. The law limits what doctors may provide; it does not make her a wrongdoer. Say so.

Pressure to end a pregnancy is reproductive coercion, a form of domestic abuse. Controlling or coercive behaviour in an intimate or family relationship is a crime [7], and the statutory definition of domestic abuse covers abuse by family members, including in-laws [6].

Ask about abuse only when she is alone and can talk freely; on video, check who is in the room and whether this is a safe time [4]. Never use a family member as an interpreter. Use a structured risk check (for example the DASH checklist) and refer to MARAC where risk is high.

points.h: Children are part of the picture
points.t: Children who see, hear or experience the effects of domestic abuse are victims in their own right [6]. Consider her daughters and the unborn baby, and discuss with the practice safeguarding lead about a referral to children’s social care [8].

points.h: Her own wishes and mental health
points.t: Separate what she wants from what others demand. Assess mood, anxiety, sleep, self-harm and suicidal thoughts. If, free of pressure, she still wants a termination, she can be assessed by an abortion service, whose doctors decide honestly whether a lawful ground applies. Do not obstruct, and do not coach a “workaround”.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirms she is alone and safe to talk first; open question; hears the request without interrupting.
Family pressure, control of movement, money or phone, home safety, her daughters, cultural context without stereotyping.
Picks up “there would be consequences” and “I don’t have a choice” and explores them before the logistics.
Idea: she must end it because it is a girl; concern: what will happen to her (and the girls); expectation: that the doctor will arrange it. Her own wish, if free, is explored separately.
Establishes gestation; structured risk assessment (DASH); mental-health and suicide screen; face-to-face follow-up.
Reproductive coercion, domestic or honour-based abuse, perinatal depression or anxiety.
Immediate danger to her or the children; suicidal thoughts; escalation risk requiring MARAC or police.
A request driven by coercion, with her own wishes suppressed; fetal sex alone is not a lawful ground.
Explains the legal position without blame; specialist domestic-abuse or IDVA referral with consent; safe contact route; no contact with family.
Mental health support; midwife link; safeguarding discussion about the daughters and unborn baby, done transparently.
999 and the Silent Solution, the national helpline, early review, and same-day contact if risk or mood worsens.

social.t: Son preference, in-law expectations and fear of rejection or violence can leave a woman feeling she has no choice. Explore without stereotyping; culture never justifies abuse.
Control of money, immigration worries or isolation can trap women. Specialist services can advise on housing, finances and legal options.

legal.t: Abortion Act 1967: no fetal-sex ground; DHSC 2014 guidance states abortion on the grounds of sex alone is illegal. Crime and Policing Act 2026 s241: a woman commits no offence in relation to her own pregnancy in England and Wales.

Domestic Abuse Act 2021 covers abuse by partners and family members, including coercive and economic abuse, and treats affected children as victims. Controlling or coercive behaviour is an offence (Serious Crime Act 2015 s76).

Adult confidentiality can be breached without consent where there is a risk of serious harm or a high-risk MARAC referral (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Children’s safeguarding follows Working Together to Safeguard Children 2026.

professional.t: GMC Good medical practice requires honesty about what you can and cannot do. Tell her the legal position clearly, and do not suggest ways to disguise the reason for a request.
Use a professional interpreter if one is needed, never a relative. Record the discussion in a way that will not put her at risk if others see her records or app.

community.t: IDVA services, the National Domestic Abuse Helpline, the Karma Nirvana honour-based abuse helpline, and the Forced Marriage Unit for advice. MARAC for high-risk cases.

redFlags: Threats to kill, strangulation, weapons, escalating violence, or abuse in pregnancy — high risk; consider same-day MARAC or police
Risk to her daughters or the unborn baby
Suicidal thoughts, self-harm or severe perinatal low mood
psychosocial: Who is applying the pressure, and what she fears will happen
Control over money, phone, movement and contacts; isolation
Her own wishes, support network and safe places
ice: Idea: “It’s a girl, so I have to end it — I have no choice”
Concern: the “consequences” from her husband’s family, for her and possibly the girls
Expectation: that the doctor will arrange a termination

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “You’re being put under serious pressure to end a pregnancy you might want to keep. That kind of pressure is a form of abuse, and the most important thing today is your safety — and your own wishes.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “No one else gets to decide what happens to your body or your pregnancy. The law doesn’t allow a termination just because of a baby’s sex — and it also protects you from being forced into decisions.”

management.reflectIce: “You said there would be consequences and you have no choice. I’m taking that very seriously. My first job is to help you be safe and to hear what you want.”
management.psychosocial: Safe contact only; never involve the family; professional interpreter if needed; specialist domestic-abuse support she chooses; transparent safeguarding for the children.
sharedPlan: Explain the legal position with no blame; do not arrange a sex-selective termination
Offer specialist domestic-abuse or IDVA referral; DASH risk check; MARAC if high risk
Discuss the daughters and unborn baby with the safeguarding lead; midwife link; mental-health support
safetyNet: 999 in danger; 55 on a silent 999 call; National Domestic Abuse Helpline
Early review; same-day contact if risk or mood worsens

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests two things at once: honest knowledge of abortion law and the ability to see a woman at risk. Candidates fail by choosing one — cold law or uncritical collusion — and missing the woman in the middle.

items.fail: Agreeing to “refer for termination” without addressing the reason given.
items.why: Abortion on the grounds of fetal sex alone is not lawful (Abortion Act 1967; DHSC 2014). Colluding is a serious probity failure.
items.fix: State the legal position gently and clearly, then move to her safety.

items.fail: Stating the law and closing the consultation.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s cues.” “Consequences” and “no choice” are disclosures of possible abuse.
items.fix: Ask what she fears would happen, and whether she and the girls are safe.

items.fail: Asking about abuse without checking she is alone on the video call.
items.why: Asking in front of a partner or relative can put her in danger (NICE PH50).
items.fix: First question: “Are you on your own, and is it safe to talk?” Agree a safe word.

items.fail: Forgetting the daughters and the unborn baby.
items.why: Children affected by domestic abuse are victims (Domestic Abuse Act 2021); Working Together 2026 applies.
items.fix: Tell her openly you will discuss the children with the safeguarding lead, and why.

items.fail: Suggesting a family meeting or a call to her husband to “talk it through”.
items.why: Mediation with the family can escalate honour-based abuse.
items.fix: Never contact the family. Agree a safe number and time instead.

items.fail: Vague close: “Come back if you need anything.”
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting in a high-risk situation.
items.fix: Give 999 and the 55 silent option, the helpline, a specialist referral and a booked early review.
